claims.statement: The EDPB's 2026 consultation guidelines say a controller can obtain broad consent for future projects within defined areas of scientific research when additional safeguards and recognized ethical standards are used; dynamic project-by-project consent is another route. A recontactable research cohort is therefore legally conceivable, but consent design and ongoing governance are substantive work rather than a one-time checkbox.

Participant consent authorizes defined processing but does not by itself prove that the founder will own exclusive cross-sponsor commercialization rights. Those rights would also have to survive controller roles, sponsor and clinical-site contracts, data-subject rights, and the applicable EHDS/GDPR route; no evidence establishes those allocations for this candidate.

The EHDS framework covers secondary use of research and wearable-generated health data, uses data permits and secure processing environments, gives individuals an opt-out, and phases most secondary-use rules in from 2029. It should make governed health data more findable and accessible, so generic cohort data scarcity is a weaker long-run moat than protocol-specific longitudinal linkage, quality, and recontact capability.

FDA guidance requires a digital health technology used for remote trial data acquisition to be fit for purpose, including adequate verification, validation, usability, participant suitability, data integrity, and meaningful interpretation. EMA likewise treats wearable-derived clinical variables, endpoint reliability, accuracy, sensitivity to change, clinical validity, and relevance to benefit-risk assessment as matters that can fall within its qualification remit.

A 2025 regulatory review reports that novel digital endpoints can require multiple prospective studies, early health-authority consultation, technical and clinical validation, patient-meaningfulness evidence, privacy assessment, and sometimes device conformity evidence; the evidentiary bar is highest for primary endpoints or label claims. Formal qualification is voluntary, but it is described as costly, complex, multidisciplinary, and better suited to consortia in many cases.

No located evidence shows that a 30-100-person Polish cohort would be sufficient for any specific fatigue or cognitive endpoint, target population, endpoint hierarchy, or regulator. It could be adequate for feasibility or exploratory validation, but sufficiency depends on the defined context of use, measurement error, effect size, reference standard, population heterogeneity, and sponsor decision.

A 2024 peer-reviewed Tufts/DiMe analysis estimated positive sponsor value from digital endpoints: phase II incremental expected net present value of USD 2.2-3.3 million with 32-48% ROI and phase III value of USD 27-40 million with ROI four to six times the investment. This supports a real economic reason for some sponsors to fund endpoint work.

In the same study's small industry survey, ten developer responses reported sponsor agreement values with a median of USD 586,039 and mean of USD 783,258, while twelve sponsor cases reported median digital-endpoint implementation cost of USD 1 million. The sample is small and likely reflects established measures and vendors, but it is direct evidence that the category can command substantial budgets.

The candidate's 40,000 PLN starting-capital assumption is credible only for a sponsor-prepaid narrow pilot, not for independently developing a broadly qualified endpoint asset. Seven developer cases in the Tufts/DiMe survey ranged from USD 348,429 to USD 120,988,950 in development cost, with a USD 3,791,378 median; the candidate must keep participant, device, clinical, and regulatory costs contract-funded.

A 2024 analysis of pharmaceutical- and medical-device-sponsored trials found uptake of digital health technologies remained tepid and leaned toward conventional hardware such as Holter monitors and glucose meters rather than newer activity monitors and apps. Buyer interest therefore does not imply urgent or broad adoption of novel neurocognitive wearable endpoints.

No public evidence establishes renewal rates, procurement cycle, CAC, sales conversion, gross margin, or a repeatable benchmark-data licence for a new Warsaw micro-study operator. Published contract values show category spend, while incumbent product pages show repeatable platform models, but neither demonstrates that this candidate can acquire or retain customers.

Clario already markets end-to-end endpoint technology and scientific services, including more than 140 validated precision-motion outcome measures; it reports experience across more than 30,000 trial opportunities, 700 FDA/EMA drug approvals, and 100 countries. Sponsors can buy a proven integrated substitute rather than assemble a small validation site.

Koneksa markets a patented, sensor-agnostic platform plus study design, remote capture, validated digital endpoints, regulatory-grade curation, data science, SaaS licensing, and expert services; it reports more than 50 clinical programs across more than 55 countries. This directly overlaps both the proposed service wedge and the proposed transition to a licensable data/protocol platform.

In June 2026 Samsung and digital-first CRO Alcedis announced a partnership combining Galaxy wearable biosensors, clinically validated measurements, biomarker-development expertise, and clinical-research infrastructure. This is recent direct evidence that device makers and CROs can bundle the bridge from raw wearable signals to trial evidence, compressing the candidate's differentiation.

Poland's National Institute of Public Health bioethics commission states that medical experiments involving people, including questionnaire research, are reviewed for scientific feasibility, participant selection, qualified personnel, technical conditions, participant information, and consent. It also states that a medical experiment is led by a suitably qualified physician. Whether a given validation protocol is legally classified this way needs counsel, but a clinical/ethics partner is a real dependency when it is.

The 2025 regulatory review warns that wearable hardware, software, or algorithm changes during a trial can invalidate results and trigger additional verification or validation; it recommends vendor change-control and contingency plans. Unless the business controls the device and algorithm, its endpoint evidence remains dependent on a third-party manufacturer.

The candidate does not yet own the full critical mechanism: regulator-credible validity depends on the wearable and algorithm, reference instrument, clinical population, ethics and privacy governance, and sponsor-accepted context of use. The founder could own analysis code and a protocol, but a compounding asset exists only if contracts also allocate reusable data, derived-model, publication, and recontact rights.

A 30-100-person first cohort is more likely to be a learning asset than a moat. A defensible data asset would have to compound through standardized longitudinal follow-up, rare or decision-relevant reference labels, reliable versioning, cross-study comparability, and recontact; incumbents already possess validated catalogs and global deployment data, while EHDS increases access to generic health datasets.

The founder's neuroscience, biosignal, statistics, and AI background fits protocol analytics, but participant operations, physician leadership where required, ethics, privacy, quality systems, and sponsor communication are not delegable to software alone. Part-time execution is plausible only with a contracted clinical operator and a sponsor-funded scope that keeps the founder focused on design and analysis.

No evidence confirms that a wearable maker, biotech sponsor, or CRO will trust and procure a first study from this founder before the business has GCP-quality processes, a clinical partner, a disease-specific principal investigator, or prior sponsor references. The proposed partner-referral and direct-outreach distribution route remains unvalidated.

contrary_evidence: Clario reports more than 140 validated motion outcomes, more than 30,000 trial opportunities, 700 FDA/EMA drug approvals, and operations in more than 100 countries, making a full-stack incumbent an immediately available substitute.

Koneksa already combines remote-study design, a patented sensor-agnostic platform, validated endpoints, regulatory curation, analytics, and modular SaaS licensing across more than 50 clinical programs and 55 countries.

Samsung's June 2026 partnership with CRO Alcedis bundles wearable hardware, clinically validated measurements, biomarker-development expertise, and research infrastructure, showing an active device-maker/CRO response to the same gap.

A 2025 regulatory review says novel endpoint acceptance can require multiple prospective studies and early regulator consultation, with the highest evidentiary bar for primary endpoints or label claims.

The 2024 Tufts/DiMe survey found median digital-measure development cost of USD 3.79 million in seven developer cases, far above the candidate's 40,000 PLN capital assumption unless a sponsor fully prepays a narrow pilot.

A 2024 sponsor-trial analysis found tepid DHT uptake and preference for conventional devices, contradicting any assumption that buyer urgency for novel wearable neurocognitive endpoints is already broad.

EHDS is designed to make research and wearable health data available for governed secondary use, while EDPB research-consent guidance requires continuing safeguards; a consented cohort is therefore not automatically an exclusive proprietary asset.

Whether a sponsor, CRO, clinical site, ethics body, and participants will permit the founder to retain cross-sponsor data, derived-model, protocol, publication, and recontact rights.
Whether 30-100 participants provide adequate precision, representativeness, longitudinal duration, and subgroup coverage for the exact endpoint and context of use.

Whether the planned protocol is a Polish medical experiment, clinical investigation, observational study, or another category, and the resulting ethics, insurance, physician-leadership, and regulatory cost and timeline.
Whether the chosen wearable exposes stable raw data and frozen algorithms under contractual change control, and whether the reference test can be licensed for commercial cross-sponsor work.
Sponsor procurement cycle, acceptable vendor credentials, security and quality-system requirements, pricing for a first pilot, and the founder's route to a first credible reference customer.
Gross margin after participant compensation, physician and site fees, ethics and insurance, devices, reference tests, data engineering, quality documentation, and sponsor support.
Renewal probability, cross-population reuse rate, data-licensing willingness, CAC, payback, and the number of sponsor-funded studies needed before the cohort becomes meaningfully differentiated.
Recruitment speed, adherence, dropout, willingness to be recontacted, and consent-withdrawal rates for a Warsaw neurocognitive cohort.
Whether the founder can keep sponsor communication, audit readiness, and study oversight within five hours per day while retaining a full-time job.
